title: Should algorithms decide who gets seen first?

turns.speaker: Tariq
turns.text: The trust is using a model to prioritise the surgical waiting list. Clinical need, waiting time, deterioration risk.

turns.speaker: Noa
turns.text: Which is what a consultant does already, only inconsistently and at eleven at night.

turns.speaker: Ewan
turns.text: That's the strongest argument for it, honestly. The comparison isn't a perfect decision, it's a tired human one.

turns.speaker: Tariq
turns.text: The worry is what goes into it. If the training data reflects who got treated quickly before, it learns the old bias.

turns.speaker: Noa
turns.text: There's a well-known case where an algorithm used past spending as a proxy for need, and less had been spent on some patients historically.

turns.speaker: Noa
turns.text: So it concluded they were healthier, when it had really measured who had been neglected.

turns.speaker: Ewan
turns.text: Which is a data problem rather than an algorithm problem, though the effect is the same.

turns.speaker: Tariq
turns.text: The difference from a biased consultant is scale. One consultant is wrong in one hospital.

turns.speaker: Ewan
turns.text: And consistency cuts both ways. A consistent system is auditable, which a hundred individual judgements are not.

turns.speaker: Noa
turns.text: That's the part I'd hold onto. You can test a model for disparate outcomes. You cannot test a memory.

turns.speaker: Tariq
turns.text: Provided somebody is required to run that test and publish it.

turns.speaker: Ewan
turns.text: Which is the whole governance question and it's always the underfunded bit.

turns.speaker: Noa
turns.text: An override matters too, with a written reason, so the clinician stays accountable rather than deferring.

points: A hospital trust is using a model to prioritise surgical waiting lists.
Ewan argues the fair comparison is not a perfect decision but an inconsistent, tired human one.
Tariq warns training data can encode historical bias.
Noa cites a case where past spending was used as a proxy for need, so under-treated patients were classified as healthier.
Scale distinguishes algorithmic from individual bias, though consistency also makes systems auditable in ways human judgement is not.
They conclude governance is decisive: mandatory published testing for disparate outcomes, plus a clinician override requiring a written reason.
